arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Hungar argued that the opposing side seeks to circumvent statutory limitations by manufacturing a parallel mechanism for relief.
Mr. Armstrong stated that a cost recovery action is an equitable action for restitution without a jury trial.
Mr. Geck noted that more than 400,000 contaminated sites require the work of private parties for cleanup.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of a federal cleanup statute. It asks if a liable party can sue other liable parties for cost recovery.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on April 23, 2007.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to bar the opposing side from using the cost recovery statute against other liable parties.
the opposing side wants the Court to allow the use of the cost recovery statute to recover costs from other liable parties.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues that Congress created a specific mechanism for liable parties to share costs, which limits their options.
the opposing side argues that the cost recovery statute allows any private party to seek restitution for cleanup expenses.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Souter asked if the court must determine the innocence of the party bringing the action first.
Justice Ginsburg asked if the Court was wrong to say the statute provides a cause of action for private parties in a prior case.
